title: Practice block close
hookLine: building your own way closes the way King Josiah renewed a covenant: by reading it aloud
tomorrow: why wouldn't a man answer the rabbis who came to his field?

lines: A SCROLL FOUND IN THE TEMPLE.
cards: Some promises only count when they're said out loud: a wedding vow, an oath at a citizenship ceremony, even a toast. The book of Kings tells of a scroll found during repairs to the temple in Jerusalem.
The high priest tells the king's scribe, in the King James Version: "I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD." It's read to King Josiah, and when he hears it, he tears his clothes.

teach.h: READ IN THE EARS OF ALL.
teach.b: Then he goes further. He gathers priests, prophets and all the people, small and great, and "he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant." He stands by a pillar and binds himself to keep it.

teach.h: THE PEOPLE STOOD TO THE COVENANT.
teach.b: And the text adds: "And all the people stood to the covenant."

That's a thread in Jewish life: the covenant is renewed by hearing it, together. Deuteronomy commands a public reading of the law before all Israel, and in synagogues the Torah is still read aloud to the gathered people.
A text kept in a drawer can be forgotten.
A text read aloud is a promise with witnesses, even if the only witness is you. So this block closes Josiah's way. Look back at what built the last stretch.
Ready for now, leaves and all. Where I am, a guest and at home. Go and see.
Ask them. Tag the source. An invitation, never a push.

teach.h: READ IT ALOUD; IT BECOMES YOURS.
teach.b: But read aloud, it becomes yours.

how: In the synagogue the Torah is read aloud to the congregation, and Deuteronomy 31 commands a public reading of the law before all Israel. On a personal path, a finished rule can be read aloud once, to oneself or to a trusted friend, as a way of taking it on.

o: the end of building your own way, with your rule read aloud

s: in 2 Kings, the book of the law is found in the temple
"I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD."
Josiah read the scroll privately and kept it in the palace
he read it in the ears of all the people, small and great.
a written rule binds you just as much if it's never said aloud
in this story the covenant is renewed by hearing it read, together.

games.q: your sister wrote vows for her wedding, but now wants to hand her partner the card instead of saying them. what does Josiah's story suggest?
o: say them aloud: a promise read out, with witnesses, binds differently.
hand over the card; written words are already final.
skip the vows; real promises should stay private.
games.why: Josiah didn't keep the scroll on a shelf. he read it in the ears of all the people, and they stood to the covenant.

practice: Hold the clean copy of your rule and read it aloud once, slowly, in a speaking voice, as if someone you trust were listening. Then sit quietly with the last line still in the air.

wordCard.voice: Practice block close: the end of building your own way, and your rule, read aloud. Like Josiah's covenant: heard, then kept.
